title: Delay isn't refusal
hookLine: don't despair when a gift is delayed after insistent prayer: He answers in what He chooses for you (Hikam 6, paraphrased)
tomorrow: who put the wanting in you in the first place?

lines: WHAT KIND OF PROMISE IS THAT?
cards: The tracking page says in transit, and hasn't changed. The text says seen, with no reply. The portal says your application has been deferred: not yes, not no, later.
Waiting has a lot of new names. Ibn Ata'illah wrote one line about it, and it has a strange detail in it. He promises you an answer.
Then, in the same breath, he says it may not be the answer you asked for, and it may not come when you asked. So what kind of promise is that?

teach.b: Saying six of the Hikam, paraphrased: don't let the delay of a gift, after you've asked and asked, push you into despair.
He has promised to answer you in what He chooses for you, not in what you choose for yourself, and at the time He wants, not the time you want. Here's how the puzzle comes apart.

teach.h: THE ASKING, AND THE THING ASKED.
teach.b: Every dua, every personal prayer, has two parts: the asking, and the thing asked for. The promise covers the first. The Qur'an says your Lord tells you to call on Him, and He will answer.
The second part, the exact gift and the exact hour, is left open. A hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad spells out the shapes an answer can take.
When someone asks God for something good, one of three things happens: it's given soon, or it's saved for them in the next life, or a harm of the same size is turned away from them.

Three shapes of yes, and none of them is silence. Al-Bukhari keeps the warning that goes with it. A prayer is answered as long as the person doesn't grow impatient and say: I prayed, and I wasn't answered.
So the one place the conversation can close is on your side, when you stop asking. A no from a person ends a talk. Here, the talk stays open.

how: Muslims are taught to keep making dua even when an answer seems slow, following the hadith in al-Bukhari that a prayer is answered as long as the person doesn't say 'I prayed and wasn't answered.'

o: a late answer to prayer that isn't a no
a prayer that was said the wrong way
a polite way God turns down a request

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: in what He chooses, when He chooses
three shapes an answer can take

s: if a prayer isn't answered quickly, the answer is no
Ibn Ata'illah: delay isn't refusal. the answer comes in His choice and His time.
a hadith in al-Bukhari warns against saying 'I prayed and wasn't answered'
the prayer is answered as long as the person doesn't give up impatiently.
the Hikam promises you'll get exactly what you asked for if you keep asking
it promises an answer in what He chooses for you, not what you choose.

games.q: your little cousin prayed every night for a puppy. his parents said 'maybe next year.' now he says God ignored him. what's closest to Ibn Ata'illah?
o: God said no, so it's better to stop asking and move on.
he was heard; the answer may come later, or in a different shape.
he must have used the wrong words; he should pray differently.
games.why: the Hikam promises an answer in what He chooses and when; the hadith in Ahmad names three shapes it can take. the asking wasn't wasted.

practice: Take a pen and write down one thing you've stopped asking for because the waiting got long. Write it plainly, in one line, and look at it while the breath comes and goes.
If you pray, ask for it once more; if not, keep the paper somewhere you'll see it again.

wordCard.voice: Delay isn't refusal: Ibn Ata'illah's sixth saying. The answer comes in what He chooses, at the time He chooses.

orig.note: Arabic: calling on God, asking; the word for personal prayer in your own words.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: delayed, not denied, and the asking itself is never wasted. Four sayings in, two to go.

sources.ref: Ibn Ata'illah al-Iskandari, al-Hikam, aphorism 6 (don't despair at the delay of the gift)
Qur'an 40:60 (call on Me, and I will answer you)
Musnad Ahmad 11133 (a prayer is granted, stored for the hereafter, or an equal harm is averted)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6340 (answered as long as he is not impatient, saying 'I prayed and was not answered')
